I can't tell the team which organism caused the sepsis from this report. The three most abundant non-human species are typical skin or reagent contaminants. The one large bacterial signal can't be pinned to a genus or species.

**Top non-human species (species rank, clade reads ≥ 10):**

| # | Species | Clade reads | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cutibacterium acnes | 524 | Skin commensal; the old genus name *Propionibacterium* is on the contaminant list |
| 2 | Acidovorax sp. JMULE5 | 331 | Genus *Acidovorax* is on the contaminant list |
| 3 | Staphylococcus epidermidis | 182 | Skin commensal; common contaminant from the blood draw |

Next were *E. coli* (154 reads), equine infectious anemia virus (132, which usually comes from lentiviral vector material in the lab) and *Methylorubrum extorquens* (88). Other contaminant genera also show up: *Brevundimonas* (1,473), *Ralstonia*, *Pseudomonas*, *Acinetobacter* and *Methylobacterium/Methylorubrum*.

**Why I can't identify the cause:**
- **Contamination:** at 524 reads or fewer out of 500,000 pairs (≤ 0.1%), each top species looks like contamination, not infection.
- **Unresolved family signal:** the biggest non-human signal is 44,302 reads (8.9%) in Enterobacteriaceae. Of these, 44,055 were assigned only at family level, and just 232 reached *Escherichia*. This could point to a gram-negative enteric organism, but it can't say which one. It could also be an artefact of the database or the classification.
